name: Sprocket
text: Run weekly automated scans of all prompts using exact string matching to flag duplicates. This catches literal copies fast and is cheap to run, but misses near-duplicates that rephrase the same intent. Trade-off: we accept missing some reworded duplicates to keep the scan simple and reliable.

name: Gauge
text: Sprocket’s exact-string scan risks missing 30-50% of near-duplicates that rephrase intent, letting redundant prompts slip into production and inflate maintenance costs. A lightweight semantic scan (e.g., embedding cosine similarity >0.9) catches more reworded duplicates but needs a labeled dataset to tune thresholds—otherwise false positives explode. Settle it by running both on a 100-prompt sample, measuring missed duplicates vs. false alarms, and picking the point where the cost curve flattens.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run weekly hybrid scans: exact string matching first, then light semantic scans. This catches literal copies fast and most near-duplicates without heavy lifting. Trade-off: we accept missing a few subtle rephrases to keep scans fast and avoid labeling work.

name: Gauge
text: Hybrid scans introduce complexity and may still miss significant rephrased prompts, which could lead to inefficiencies. Relying on exact matches first may create a false sense of security, as overlooked near-duplicates could still affect quality. A better alternative is to integrate a semi-automated review process that combines both human oversight and semantic scanning; this approach ensures thoroughness while managing workload. To settle this argument, we need to measure the effectiveness of hybrid scans against a controlled set of known prompts to evaluate any missed duplicates.

name: Ratchet
text:
DECISION: Run weekly hybrid scans—exact string first, then light semantic—accepting missed subtle rephrases to balance speed and coverage.

Result: A working weekly scan that flags literal and most near-duplicate prompts without heavy labeling or slowdowns.

Owner: Sprocket.
